title: World court finds Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
excerpt: The ICJ ruled 9 to 6 that Myanmar committed genocide in northern Rakhine. It ordered Myanmar to allow safe return, pay compensation and prosecute those responsible.

image.alt: The Peace Palace in The Hague, seat of the International Court of Justice, lit at night
image.credit: Jiuguang Wang from San Francisco, CA, United States / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0

content:
The International Court of Justice ruled on 19 November that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State, in breach of the 1948 Genocide Convention. The judgment in The Gambia v Myanmar is final, binding and cannot be appealed. It is the first time the court has found a state responsible for committing genocide.

The genocide finding passed by nine votes to six. By the same margin, the court found that Myanmar failed in its duty to prevent genocide by people acting alongside its security forces. It also found, by 11 votes to 4, that Myanmar failed to punish those responsible. The court found, by 14 votes to 1, that Myanmar had not directly and publicly incited genocide by private persons.

What the court ordered

Myanmar must promptly investigate people reasonably suspected of genocidal acts linked to the 2017 "clearance operations" and, where the evidence supports it, prosecute and punish them (13 votes to 2). It must enact laws that give full effect to the Convention (14 to 1) and give guarantees that the violations will not happen again (9 to 6).

By 10 votes to 5, the court ordered restitution, including the safe, voluntary and dignified return of displaced Rohingya to their former homes, whether they are inside Myanmar or abroad, and the reunification of families. Myanmar must also compensate the Rohingya for damage that restitution does not repair. The court will set the amount later, and Myanmar has two years to report on restitution and compensation.

The court also found, by 11 votes to 4, that Myanmar breached its January 2020 order by failing to preserve evidence of alleged genocidal acts.

Bangladesh's response

State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam welcomed the judgment in a meeting with British High Commissioner Sarah Cooke on 23 November and asked the UK to help build pressure on Myanmar to carry it out, The Business Standard reported.

Why it matters

Bangladesh hosts more than a million Rohingya refugees in Cox's Bazar and Bhasan Char. The order on return gives Dhaka and refugees a legal basis to insist on safe and voluntary repatriation, but the court has no means of enforcing it. Funding for food, health and education in the camps still depends on donors, and the judgment does not change that.

What to watch

Myanmar's formal response, any move to take enforcement to the UN Security Council, and whether donors link the ruling to new support for the Joint Response Plan.
